# Weekly earnings of employees

In this exercise, you will recreate a labour market analysis by the ONS, reported in the table [EARN04: Gross weekly earnings of full-time employees \[last accessed 21/02/2025\]](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/datasets/grossweeklyearningsoffulltimeemployeesearn04). Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using data from the Quarterly Labour Force Survey.

Learning outcomes:
  
  -   To understand better how ONS earnings statistics are produced
-   To become more familiar with key variables from the QLFS
-   To learn  using  income weights appropriately

## Data

The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for October-December 2024.

To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: [Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024](http://doi.org/10.5255/UKDA-SN-9349-3).

## Get set up

We suggest that you create a folder named `LFS_exercises` as the working directory for this exercise -- where syntax files and other materials will be stored. After downloading the data, save it in an easily accessible location within `LFS_exercises`, such as a subfolder named `Data`.

We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let's load the packages that are are going to need:

```{r libraries}
library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation 
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions 
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data
```

Let's open the dataset.

```{r open, eval=c(-2,-5)}
setwd ("~")

### Importing a Stata format dataset 
lfs_od24 <- read_dta(
  "Data/lfs/UKDA-9349-stata/stata/stata13/lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta"
) 
```

As there are many variables in the LFS, let's create a data frame with just those required for this exercise. We also  convert the original variables  into factors in order to make them easier to manipulate. 

```{r mydata}
dataex2 <- lfs_od24 |> 
  select(PERSNO, PIWT24, PWT24,GRSSWK, INECAC05, 
         ILODEFR,FTPT, HOURPAY, SEX) |>
  mutate(
     across(
         c(INECAC05,ILODEFR,FTPT,SEX),\(x) as_factor(x, "both")
               ),
     across(
          c(GRSSWK,HOURPAY),\(x) as.numeric(x, "both")
    )
         ) 
```


## Let's examine the dataset

We can  again use `head()` or `View()` in order to inspect the data and the new variables:
  
```{r inspect}
head(dataex2)

# View(dataex2) ## Visualising the data as worksheet
```

## Examine weekly earnings

Let's examine the descriptive statistics for weekly earnings.


```{r desc1}
summary(dataex2$GRSSWK)
skimr::skim(dataex2$GRSSWK)

```
Non responses are coded using negative values, which affects analysis results. Let's do it again, this time with respondents who provided a valid answer only: 
  
```{r desc2}
s<-dataex2|>select(GRSSWK)|>
  filter(GRSSWK>0)|> 
  skimr::skim()

# Alternative: summary(dataex2$GRSSWK[dataex2$GRSSWK>0])
```


We get a first sense that the sample mean and median gross weekly earnings revolve around respectively `{r} paste0("£",round(s$numeric.mean))` and `{r} paste0("£",round(s$numeric.p50))` . Given that the mean is likely to be influenced by very large earnings, we will use the median for the rest of this exercise.

Let's now visualise the distribution of weekly earnings in the sample  using a histogram. Earnings data tend to be skewed to the right (a  small number of respondents have very large earnings) which reduces the visibility of lower earnings. We will therefore be leaving out the 1% highest earners for this exercise. 


```{r quantil}

### Finding the 99th percentile  of earnings  in the sample
q99s<-quantile(dataex2$GRSSWK[dataex2$GRSSWK>0],.99)

q99s

hist(dataex2$GRSSWK[dataex2$GRSSWK>0 & dataex2$GRSSWK<=q99s],
     main="Sample distribution of gross weekly earnings -- QLFS OD 2024",
     xlab="Earnings (£) -- 1st-99th percentiles")

```


## Inferring median earnings for the UK population

```{r histpop}
### First, we need to declare the survey design
### In this case, we only have the weights
### For earnings-related estimation we need to use PIWT24
### For other estimates - PWT24

dataex2.s<-   dataex2|> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PIWT24)

### Inference to the UK population
qtl.g<-svyquantile(~GRSSWK,
                   dataex2.s,
                   .99,
                   ci=T)

qtl.g 

qtl.gn<-qtl.g$GRSSWK[[1]]

qtl.gn
```
We now know that on average 99% of earners in the UK earn less than `{r} paste0("£", prettyNum(qtl.gn, big.mark=","))` per week. 
 Let's compare the weighted and unweighted distribution


```{r plot}

svyhist(~GRSSWK,
        subset(dataex2.s,  GRSSWK>0 & GRSSWK<qtl.gn),
        xlab="Earnings (£) -- 1st-99th percentiles", # x axis label
        main="Gross Weekly Earnings in the UK - Oct-Dec 2024", # Plot title
        freq=F)  # Print probabilities rather than frequencies

```



::: panel-tabset
## Question

Plot the distribution of hourly earnings  up to the 99th percentile in the UK between October and December 2024.

## Answer
```{r hourly}
dataex2.s<-update(dataex2.s, HOURPAY=as.numeric(HOURPAY))
quantile(dataex2$HOURPAY[dataex2$HOURPAY>0],.99)

qtl.h<-svyquantile(~HOURPAY,dataex2.s,.99,ci=T)
qtl.h

qtl.hn<-qtl.h$HOURPAY[[1]]
qtl.hn

hist(dataex2$HOURPAY[dataex2$HOURPAY>0 & dataex2$HOURPAY<68.8],     
     main="Sample distribution of net hourly earnings -- QLFS OD 2024",
     xlab="Earnings (£) -- 1st-99th percentiles")
                                                       

svyhist(~HOURPAY,subset(dataex2.s, HOURPAY>0 & HOURPAY<=qtl.hn),
        xlab="Earnings (£) -- 1st-99th percentiles",                                               
        main="Net hourly earnings in the UK, October-December 2024", 
        freq=F
)

```
:::
  
  
  
  
  
## ONS estimates for employees' gross weekly earnings
  
  The code below recreates the ONS results showing the distribution of income for full-time employees overall and by gender. 
It does it in two stages:
  
  1. First, we create a variable to flag the ONS' definition of full-time employees.    It may be a good idea to double check the definition used by the ONS [in its publication.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/datasets/grossweeklyearningsoffulltimeemployeesearn04). Looking at the notes under the Table EARN04, we learn that ONS figures are only computed for  respondents' main job, and also that *those earnings more than £100 per hour* are excluded. 

We need to  remain mindful of definitions:
  
- *Employees* refers to people who whose jobs implies working under an employment contract for an employer; 
- *Employed* refers both to people who are   employees and self employed ie who have a paid job.
- *Full-time or part-time* refer to people's self declared working-time status, irrespective of whether they are employed or self-employed. It is usually considered in the UK that part-time hours correspond to less than 30 hours per week.

LFS  data provides the INECAC05 variable, which records all nuances of economic activity (there are 35 of them!), including employment and self-employment. 
We will now examine compute the flagging variable and examine its  distribution  in the sample.

```{r ftEmp}

dataex2<-dataex2 |> 
             mutate(
                  ftEmp=ifelse(
                         (FTPT=="[3] New Deal-FT" | FTPT=="[1] Full time") & 
                         HOURPAY<=100 &
                         INECAC05=="[1] Employee",
                         "Full-time employee", 
                         "Anything else"
                               ),
                  ftEmp=as.factor(ftEmp)
                   )
                  
table(dataex2$ftEmp)
```

2. We then create a version of the data that takes the income weights into account and compute the results:


```{r svy}
dataex2.s<-   dataex2|> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PIWT24)


medinc=dataex2.s|>group_by(ftEmp)|> 
           summarise(test=
                     survey_quantile(GRSSWK,
                     quantiles=.5,               
                     vartype="ci"))

medinc
```

The median weekly earnings of  full-time employees in the UK in October-December 2024 ranged between  £`{r} round(medinc[[2,3]],1)` and £`{r}  round(medinc[[2,4]],1)`. We need to keep in mind that by using the income weights, those with missing values on GRSSWK are automatically left out. 


::: panel-tabset
## Questions

1.  What are the median weekly earnings for men and women in the UK?

2.  What are median hourly earnings in  the highest  decile for males and females  in the UK? How does it compare with the lowest decile?

3. Why are we using a different weight from exercise 1?


## Answers

1.  

```{r answer1}


medinc.sex<-dataex2.s|>group_by(ftEmp,SEX)|>
           summarise(Medwk=
                     survey_quantile(GRSSWK,
                     quantiles=.5,               
                     vartype="ci"))

medinc.sex
```

Median weekly earnings for men and women in the UK ranged respectively between £`{r} round(medinc.sex$Medwk_q50_low[3],1)` - £`{r} round(medinc.sex$Medwk_q50_upp[3],1)` and £`{r} round(medinc.sex$Medwk_q50_low[4],1)` - £`{r} round(medinc.sex$Medwk_q50_upp[4],1)`

2.  

```{r answer2}
inc10.sex<-dataex2.s|>group_by(ftEmp,SEX)|>
           summarise(NHrPay=
                     survey_quantile(HOURPAY,
                     quantiles=.1,               
                     vartype="ci"))


inc10.sex

inc90.sex<-dataex2.s|>group_by(ftEmp,SEX)|>
           summarise(NHrPay=
                     survey_quantile(HOURPAY,
                     quantiles=.9,               
                     vartype="ci"))


```
The  net hourly rate of pay  for men and women in the highest decile in the UK ranged  respectively between £`{r} round(inc90.sex$NHrPay_q90_low[3],1)` - £`{r} round(inc90.sex$NHrPay_q90_upp[3],1)` and £`{r} round(inc90.sex$NHrPay_q90_low[4],1)` - £`{r} round(inc90.sex$NHrPay_q90_upp[4],1)`. In the lowest decide, hourly rates of pay were  identical. 


3. Because earnings are computed for a specific subpopulation: those in employment with valid earnings data.

:::
